description: Cometlings Crew is a team of four who built Cometworks, a space mission design game made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are passionate about game development, orbital mechanics and making space science accessible to students. Our team is complete, so we are not recruiting new members. Thanks for checking out our project!
summary:
Cometworks is a cosy voxel space-agency tycoon in which players design, manage and simulate a complete space mission. Players run a tiny agency of Cometlings, small and curious voxel creatures, on an island campus, and take on missions with NASA-style briefings. For each mission, they choose instruments, build the spacecraft piece by piece, select an orbit and a launch vehicle, and fly the mission using orbital mechanics based on real formulas. Mass, power, budget, data, communications and mission time are limited, so every choice has consequences that players can see and evaluate. The finish line is the comet Mother-Ice, an old, icy, shining comet that passes Earth at the end of the campaign.

The game addresses the challenge by turning mission trade-offs into decisions students can test, and it is designed for players with no prior space knowledge. It uses real planetary data from JPL and NSSDCA for its orbits and masses, so the trade-offs it teaches reflect real mission design.
details:
Every space mission is a set of trade-offs: a better instrument needs more power, a higher orbit needs more fuel, and every kilogram competes with the budget. Cometworks lets students experience that balance from start to finish. Players lead a crew of Cometlings through a 25-year campaign against rival agencies. Each mission starts with a briefing inspired by a real NASA science question, like “Does the Moon shake?”. The player chooses a target, payload and team, matures the concept in a design review, builds the rocket part by part, and launches it on real orbital mechanics.

You can watch the whole flight, speed it up, or skip to the end and get a comic recap that explains why it went the way it did. Later, you can drive rovers on the Moon, Mars and Europa, and visit a fair where rival agencies and space-science “Legends” trade stories.

How we used NASA’s resources

We built the game around the materials in the challenge:

  • The design review follows the Concept Maturity Levels framework from NASA JPL.
  • Every mission is split into the four segments from “Design and Develop Science Missions”: launch, space, ground and user.
  • Instruments have to fit the science goal, as in “A Learning Game About Telescopes”.
  • Trajectory planning and the 3D solar-system map are inspired by GMAT and NASA Mission Viz.
  • An in-game Mission Design Lab stand explains NASA Goddard’s study levels.
  • The sky runs on NASA open data: JPL Solar System Dynamics for planet orbits and gravity, and NSSDCA fact sheets for planet sizes, rotation and gravity.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission design usually lives in papers and professional tools that feel out of reach. We wanted anyone, from a curious kid to a university student, to feel what it’s like to turn a science question into a mission, and to learn why trade-offs, margins and maturity reviews matter. The goal is to spark interest in space careers and make NASA’s own methods feel approachable and fun.

Tools we used

Godot Engine 4.6 with GDScript, and Jolt Physics for the flight model. ffmpeg for video, and Git and GitHub for version control. We developed and tested everything on regular laptops, since integrated graphics is our target hardware.

What makes it creative

Real orbital mechanics and NASA frameworks sit behind a soft, cozy art style. Missions are written as small puzzles: the briefing hides the technical requirements, and you deduce them. Your crew remembers the missions they worked on, and every flight can become a comic.

What we considered

  • Accessibility: a colour-blind mode, key remapping, graphics presets for older computers, reduced motion, and full English and Portuguese support.
  • Honesty about NASA: the game clearly separates what it models from what it uses. NASA data is labeled as used; NASA tools and methods are labeled as inspiration.
  • Learning curve: a gentle tutorial that unlocks the menus a few at a time, so newcomers aren’t overwhelmed and experienced players can switch everything on from the start.
